title: How 'Choosin' Texas' Became the Longest-Running No. 1 Hit Ever
summary:
This week, for the 23rd time, Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' sits at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Those 23 nonconsecutive weeks are an all-time record, beating Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You,' which hit 22 weeks just last December.

So how did a lonesome, twangy country ballad about losing a guy to a pretty stranger become the biggest chart-topper ever? NPR points to five reasons.

First, it's a genuinely good song. It references 'Amarillo by Morning,' and it feels timeless — you could imagine it being sung by Tammy Wynette. It's catchy and relatable.

Second, the country audience has shifted from radio to streaming. In recent years, country-adjacent songs like Lil Nas X's 'Old Town Road' and Shaboozey's 'A Bar Song (Tipsy)' also posted record-setting runs. Streaming rewards songs that get played over and over.

Third, pop music is having a down year. The top four songs on the Hot 100 last week were all country or country-adjacent. New albums by Harry Styles, Gracie Abrams, and Charli xcx failed to make the cultural dent fans expected.

Fourth, there's just so much music. With hundreds of albums released weekly, listeners and radio programmers gravitate to fewer and fewer hits. Once a song hits No. 1, its success becomes self-reinforcing.

Fifth, sales still matter. 'Choosin' Texas' has topped the Digital Song Sales chart for 18 weeks, selling thousands of copies each time. This week, it added another 6,000 copies.

Even with Taylor Swift releasing a new single, 'Patient Zero,' this Friday, 'Choosin' Texas' likely won't be interrupted until December — when Mariah Carey's Christmas classic returns.
why_it_matters: This record is a snapshot of how streaming has rewritten the music business: charts now measure repeated listening as much as a song's release moment, so a track can sit at No. 1 for months and an old Christmas song can climb back every winter. It also shows how genre walls are blurring, and how a quiet year for pop can hand country music the biggest stage in the industry.

background_read: The Billboard Hot 100 (a weekly ranking of the most popular songs in the United States, first published in 1958) now blends streaming, radio airplay and digital sales — so a song can keep climbing long after release if listeners keep pressing play. That is exactly how Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' (a holiday track from 1994 that only reached No. 1 for the first time in 2019) has been able to stack up weeks one December at a time rather than in a single run. The record for the longest continuous modern run belonged to Lil Nas X's 'Old Town Road,' which spent 19 straight weeks at No. 1 in 2019 and helped push country sounds into pop; Shaboozey's 'A Bar Song (Tipsy)' matched that run in 2024.

Ella Langley is a country singer from Alabama, and her song name-checks 'Amarillo by Morning,' a classic by George Strait. NPR compares the feel of the ballad to Tammy Wynette (one of country music's most famous voices, known for 1968's 'Stand by Your Man'), a sign of how old-fashioned and timeless critics find it.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — quality and a new audience
perspectives.description: Ella Langley's ballad is praised as a genuinely good, timeless song, and its success shows country music reaching listeners far beyond traditional country radio. For fans, it is proof that a slow, twangy track can beat big pop releases on merit rather than marketing.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / critical — a record that measures repetition
perspectives.description: A record built on 23 nonconsecutive weeks partly reflects playlists, streaming loops and a weak year for pop competitors, not simply a song everyone loves. When the decisive factor is another 6,000 copies and endless replays, the No. 1 spot says as much about chart mechanics and a December holiday surge as about popularity.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — the pattern behind the headline
perspectives.description: Country-adjacent songs like 'Old Town Road' and 'A Bar Song (Tipsy)' have been setting chart records since 2019, which suggests a structural shift rather than a one-off fluke. Music charts have always followed technology — sheet music, then radio, then downloads, now streaming — and each change redefines what 'No. 1' even means.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — what could end the run
perspectives.description: Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' arrives Friday and Mariah Carey's Christmas staple returns in December, so the streak has two clear threats on the calendar. Longer term, Billboard could adjust how it weighs streaming versus sales, and the open question is whether pop's weak year was a blip or the start of a longer country-led era.
